## Introduction

This document demonstrates how to combine Markdown text with executable Julia code chunks in Quarto, run through a Julia Jupyter kernel (via `IJulia`).

## Simulating Selection Response

A simple way to see genetic gain in action is to simulate repeated rounds of truncation selection on a normally-distributed breeding value, keeping only the top fraction of individuals each generation.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-genetic-gain
#| fig-cap: "Simulated mean breeding value over generations of truncation selection"
#| warning: false

using Random
using Statistics
using Plots

Random.seed!(42)

n_individuals = 200
n_generations = 15
selection_fraction = 0.2
heritability = 0.4

mean_bv = Float64[]
population = randn(n_individuals)
push!(mean_bv, mean(population))

for _ in 1:n_generations
    n_selected = round(Int, n_individuals * selection_fraction)
    selected = sort(population, rev = true)[1:n_selected]
    parent_mean = mean(selected)

    # Offspring regress toward the selected parents' mean, scaled by heritability,
    # plus fresh environmental/genetic noise each generation.
    global population = parent_mean .* heritability .+ randn(n_individuals) .* (1 - heritability)
    push!(mean_bv, mean(population))
end

plot(0:n_generations, mean_bv,
    xlabel = "Generation",
    ylabel = "Mean breeding value",
    title = "Response to Truncation Selection",
    legend = false,
    linewidth = 2,
    marker = :circle)
```

## Takeaway

Even this toy simulation shows the classic diminishing-returns shape of a selection response curve - genetic gain per generation is largest early on and tapers off as the population approaches the limits of its existing genetic variation.
